title: The Medium at Endor
lead: On the night before his last battle, King Saul disguised himself and asked a woman at Endor who had a ghost at her call to bring up the dead prophet Samuel. Whether Samuel truly appeared, a demon took his form, or the woman deceived Saul has been argued since antiquity.

sections.b: Saul had removed the mediums from Israel, as the law required (Leviticus 19:31; Deuteronomy 18:10–12). Facing the Philistines with no answer from God, he sought one out at Endor (1 Samuel 28:3–25). The scene is told once, but it echoes through later writings. Chronicles names it among the reasons Saul died (1 Chronicles 10:13–14). Isaiah mocks mediums whose voices whisper from the ground (Isaiah 8:19; Isaiah 29:4). Sirach says Samuel prophesied after his death. Ancient Jewish and Christian readers divided over what happened: a real Samuel (the Talmud, Justin Martyr, Origen), a demon (Tertullian, Eustathius, Gregory of Nyssa, Luther, Calvin), or a fraud (Samuel ben Hofni, Reginald Scot). The story became a fixture of art and of debates over witchcraft in early modern Europe.
